title: Second life: What happened to Jason Arday was a soviet-style tragedy
gist: A Ukrainian-born writer who grew up in the USSR compares the public 'character assassination' and death of Cambridge sociologist Jason Arday to Soviet-style collective denunciation, using Yevtushenko's poetry and the treatment of Princess Diana to argue that British society's own pile-on culture shares the same psychological mechanism as Soviet mob condemnation.

themes.theme: Collective condemnation as a recurring social mechanism

insights.claim: The Soviet propaganda phrase 'Vse kak odin' ('all as one') was used to manufacture the appearance of unanimous collective condemnation of dissidents, even by people who admitted they had never read the work they were denouncing (e.g. Solzhenitsyn, whose books had been removed from libraries and shops).
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Illustrates a reusable pattern-recognition tool for identifying manufactured consensus/pile-ons in any institutional or media environment, useful for assessing reputational-risk narratives that may be more coordinated than organic.
insights.quote: Having not read any of Solzhenitsyn's dirty writings myself, I nevertheless strongly condemn them as anti-Soviet lies and libel.

insights.claim: The author's core thesis is that collective emotion of any kind -- whether unanimous praise or compulsory denunciation -- is inherently dangerous and oppressive because it strips targets of individual agency until, in extreme cases, 'life itself starts looking meaningless.'
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: A generalizable framework for evaluating public 'cancellation' or pile-on episodes (in politics, corporate governance, or markets) as a distinct social-psychological risk category rather than a purely reputational one.
insights.quote: There's nothing more dangerous and oppressive than collective emotion—be it unanimous joy and admiration, or compulsory denunciation and dislike.

insights.claim: The author explicitly frames the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday as the result of a 'relentless character assassination' by British society and media collectively, structurally analogous to Soviet-era denunciation campaigns, though he does not detail the specific allegations against Arday.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Signals a media/public narrative in which a high-profile UK academic's downfall and death are being reframed by commentators as an indictment of British media/social-pile-on culture rather than of Arday's own conduct -- relevant for anyone tracking UK academia/culture-war reputational risk cycles.
insights.quote: I won't get into the already widely known details of his ordeal whereby he found himself on the receiving end of a relentless character assassination, justified or not as the accusations may have been.

themes.theme: Literary and historical parallels used to make the case

insights.claim: The author cites Yevgeny Yevtushenko's 1963 poem 'A Picture of Childhood,' describing a Siberian market crowd beating a hungry thief to death 'with ingenuity, with relish, with weighty righteousness,' as a literary template for how crowds justify escalating violence against a designated target.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: A mental model (mob justifies excess violence/punishment as righteous) transferable to analyzing modern 'cancel' dynamics or corporate/political scapegoating episodes.
insights.quote: And if a hundred, howling wildly, Beat one—even if he deserves it, I will never be the hundred and first!

insights.claim: The author draws a direct parallel between Arday's treatment and Princess Diana's, quoting his own 1997 Guardian column arguing Diana was 'bullied by society as a whole—the press, the politicians, the royal family and the crowd' until she 'could not cope with this brutal force.'
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Suggests the author (and by extension a segment of UK cultural commentary) sees a recurring 29-year pattern of media-driven collective bullying of prominent individuals in Britain, a lens likely to recur in future high-profile UK media controversies.
insights.quote: She was bullied by the society as a whole—the press, the politicians, the royal family and the crowd... Diana is gone. Who will be next?
